entries.title: ASEAN offers Myanmar's sidelined leaders a path back to summits, but says restrictions will stay until there is meaningful progress on its peace plan
entries.summary: Southeast Asian leaders have agreed to engage Myanmar in stages after years of excluding its leaders from high-level meetings. The bloc says Myanmar could regain full representation if it makes progress on a peace plan.
entries.content:
Myanmar

ASEAN offers sidelined Myanmar leaders path back to talks

November 15, 2026

Southeast Asian leaders have agreed to engage Myanmar in stages after years of excluding its leaders from high-level meetings. The bloc says Myanmar could regain full representation if it makes progress on a peace plan.

Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Sunday to engage Myanmar's government in stages, while making its return to high-level meetings conditional on progress on a regional peace plan.

Myanmar remains a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but its political leaders have been barred from summits and foreign ministers' meetings since October 2021.

The military seized power that year, overthrowing the elected government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi and triggering a civil war that continues today.

What did ASEAN agree on Myanmar?

In a joint statement, the leaders called for "a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground.”

They said ASEAN could gradually restore Myanmar's full political representation if it makes "sustained and concrete progress” on the bloc's five-point peace plan. The plan has yielded little since it was agreed on in 2021, and fighting continues between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups.

"What more can we do for Myanmar?” Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. asked at the leaders' retreat in Manila. He urged the bloc to find practical ways to advance the peace plan and support an inclusive process led by Myanmar.

Thailand has pushed for closer engagement since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as civilian president this year following elections that monitors dismissed as a sham.

What else is on the agenda in Manila?

Leaders are also discussing trade, regional security and ways to share fuel supplies to cope with disruptions caused by the war in Iran. Australia and the Philippines signed a defense agreement on Sunday, while Canada and the Philippines announced on Saturday that they had concluded free trade negotiations.

A proposed code of conduct for the South China Sea remains unresolved. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said negotiations between ASEAN and China were 80% complete, but diplomats told AFP a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the summit.

What is Trump expected to do in Manila?

US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive on Tuesday, toward the end of the summit, and meet the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other members of the Quad. The meeting is expected to precede talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.

Activists plan to march against Trump's visit on Tuesday. Their protest is aimed in part at a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could displace Indigenous families.



The Philippines hands the rotating ASEAN chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due to take over in 2028.

entries.title: Macron urges unity as Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia
entries.summary: Leaders of French-speaking nations gathered in Phnom Penh as a row over who should lead the Francophonie and Congo’s threat to quit put pressure on Macron to broker consensus.
entries.content:
France

Macron urges unity as Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia

November 15, 2026

Leaders of French-speaking nations gathered in Phnom Penh as a row over who should lead the Francophonie and Congo’s threat to quit put pressure on Macron to broker consensus.

A summit of French-speaking nations opened Sunday in Phnom Penh, with French President Emmanuel Macron trying to head off a walkout by the group's biggest African member over who will lead it next.

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) brings together about 90 states and governments, including 53 full members, from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Canada.

It is made up of countries that use French as an official language, former French colonies, and other states with substantial historic ties to France.

What is the disagreement about?

The OIF is set to choose its next secretary-general on Monday.

Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who has held the post since 2018, is seeking a third term. DR Congo has threatened to leave if she is re-elected, accusing Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in eastern Congo, an accusation Rwanda denies. 

DR Congo has 57.3 million French speakers, second only to France, per the OIF, so its exit would be a major blow. Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew from the association last year after their membership was suspended over coups.

On Saturday, DR Congo said it was withdrawing its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country's martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.

Kinshasa said it would back former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos to allow "consensus around a unifying candidacy."

AFP described the offer as conditional on Rwanda also stepping aside. However, Rwanda's foreign minister said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race.

What did Macron say?

Macron warned against "internal fractures" in the group.

"We must ensure that we preserve what constitutes its strength—namely, its unity," he said.

Rwanda said Macron had asked President Paul Kagame to withdraw his candidacy, which he refused. Macron's office said Paris suggested both candidates step aside.

"With that intervention we're going backwards, to the idea that France decides," a member of a non-African delegation told AFP anonymously. France is the largest donor, and Canada provides 25% of the budget.

Macron arrives amid unrest at home, where more than 600,000 people marched earlier this month over wages and in support of student protests, with thousands arrested. 

UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press Cambodia, which has been referred to as a de facto one-party state, to free detained activists. "No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions," he said.

entries.title: Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance
entries.summary: Events are being held for Volkstrauertag, a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts say the country is headed for a budget crisis. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance

Published November 14, 2026last updated November 15, 2026

Events are being held for 'Volkstrauertag,' a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts say the country is headed for a budget crisis. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The German and Austrian presidents will be speaking at events marking Volkstrauertag
  • The day commemorates soldiers and civilians who died in war but also victims of the Nazi regime persecuted for their sexual identity
  • Solar energy output in Germany is drawing close a record total of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year
  • Economics experts are warning that the country is living beyond its means
  • Health care cuts mean people might have to pay privately to avoid long waiting times, says the national association for statutory physicians
  • Experts in Germany have warned against too much reliance on a sole provider after a major outage at Microsoft affected German businesses

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on November 14, 2026:

Skip next section Berlin police file 28 criminal charges against Gen Z protesters

Berlin police file 28 criminal charges against Gen Z protesters

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.

Police said there had been some clashes with participants.



A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.  

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

Skip next section Steinmeier condemns rising antisemitism in Germany

Steinmeier condemns rising antisemitism in Germany

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country."

Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic."

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Skip next section Nuremberg overrun by sheep in annual spectacle

Nuremberg overrun by sheep in annual spectacle

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many important biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.

Skip next section Thieves drive car into jewelry shop in dramatic break-in

Thieves drive car into jewelry shop in dramatic break-in

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then said to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Skip next section Germany marks day of mourning for victims of war and oppression

Germany marks day of mourning for victims of war and oppression

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

Skip next section We are resuming our Germany coverage

We are resuming our Germany coverage

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,

Skip next section Pausing coverage from Germany

Pausing coverage from Germany

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Skip next section WATCH: From watching to acting: Germany's spy shift

WATCH: From watching to acting: Germany's spy shift

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Skip next section Bavaria holds funeral for former deputy premier Hubert Aiwanger

Bavaria holds funeral for former deputy premier Hubert Aiwanger

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

Skip next section Lufthansa largely unaffected by US flight ground stop

Lufthansa largely unaffected by US flight ground stop

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

Skip next section Far-right AfD nominates ex-footballer as presidential candidate

Far-right AfD nominates ex-footballer as presidential candidate

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has nominated Thomas Berthold, a former top football player, as its choice to be next German president.

Bertold, 62, would be a excellent choice "as president for all Germans," AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla wrote on X.

"We are sure that our candidate can be chosen far beyond any party lines," they wrote.

Berthold had a distinguished professional football career, including 64 matches with the German national team, with which he won the world championship in Italy in 2000.

He has also attained some prominence in recent years with his appearances at demonstrations opposing the government's measures to stem the coronavirus pandemic.

His role during the pandemic has been criticized by Stephan Mayer, the spokesman on sports policy of the conservative bloc led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Mayer said Berthold had "attracted notice with very questionable and crude remarks" during the crisis.

He said the ex-footballer was "without doubt an outstanding and very successful professional" player, but "not a candidate to be taken seriously for the highest office in the state."

The candidate supported by the conservative bloc, the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, Ilse Aigner of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), is widely seen as the favorite to succeed current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

The vote by a special assembly convened for the purpose is set for January 30.

Skip next section Greens approve coalition agreement in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Greens approve coalition agreement in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

The Green Party in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has given the green light to a coalition agreement negotiated with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD)and socialist Left Party.

This comes after the Left Party in the state approved the agreement on Friday.

The SPD is expected to give its stamp of approval on Saturday afternoon to the deal, which was negotiated by the three parties following September 20 elections in the state.

The incumbent state premier, Manuela Schwesig of the SPD, intends to stand for reelection on Monday.

The designated coalition will hold a total of 39 seats in the 71-seat state parliament.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which emerged as strongest single force from the election, won 32 seats and will be the only opposition party after both the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and pro-businessFree Democrats (FDP) fell beneath the 5% threshold to enter parliament.

The AfD made no attempt to form a coalition with the necessary majority, as all other parties refuse to cooperate with it.

Skip next section Experts warn against single-provider dependency

Experts warn against single-provider dependency

Experts in Germany have warned companies, schools and government authorities against reliance on a sole provider for digital services after Microsoft services suffered a major worldwide outage.

"Anyone who makes themselves unilaterally dependent on a single source for central digital technologies risks production downtimes and competitive disadvantages in an emergency," said Ralf Wintergerst, president of the industry association Bitkom.

IT security expert Christopher Kunz from the Heise Online trade magazine said such dependency posed a risk to both German society and economy "because we are not only at the mercy of Microsoft's technical competence, but also the goodwill of the US government."

"Through sanctions, it can ensure in a flash that individual organizations or even entire nations lose access to the Microsoft cloud," he said.

Manuel Atug, the founder and spokesperson for AG Kritis, an alliance of independent experts for critical infrastructures, said there were enough alternative providers from Germany or Europe to allow a diversification.

On Thursday, central services of the Microsoft 365 suite, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, began to be hit by outages worldwide, with disruptions continuing into Saturday European time.

Skip next section Budget crisis looming if spending is not cut — experts

Budget crisis looming if spending is not cut — experts

Leading economics experts have predicted a serious German budget crisis from next year if the issue of spending is not addressed.

Their remarks come as the budget committee of the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, early on Friday approved a provisional 2027 federal budget after nearly 16 hours of negotiations.

The budget foresees new debt, including loans from special funds, totalling around €210 billion ($231.5 billion).

Spending in the core budget rises to a record €561 billion, while net borrowing climbs to almost €123 billion in the core budget alone.

"This budget policy cannot be sustained in the long term," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute in Munich, told the Sunday edition of Die Welt newspaper, saying spending priorities had to be established

"All other spending should be frozen or, if possible, cut," Fuest said, adding that tax rises would be inevitable if this did not happen.

Jens Boysen-Hogrefe of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW Kiel) sees things similarly.

"Owing to economic fluctuations and special effects, there may be some breathing room in individual years, but the trend is clearly negative," he said, owing to the fact that the population is aging while interest payments are rising.

"Additional levies are likely even with strong spending discipline," he said.

Ansgar Heveling, the president of the Bundesrechnungshof, the federal audit court that monitors financial management by the government, called on the coalition government to do make more effort to consolidate the budget.

Noting that every third euro spent by the government is financed by borrowing, he said it was clear that it was living beyond its means, and warned that the share of interest spending in the federal budget would double by 2030.

Skip next section Solar energy output set for record high in Germany in 2026

Solar energy output set for record high in Germany in 2026

An above-average number of sunshine hours and the growing number of photovoltaic facilities has contributed to solar energy production that is approaching a record total for Germany, an industry association says.

By September 27, solar energy output had reached 90.2 terawatt-hours, which is already more than the 90 terawatt-hours generated for all of 2025, according to the German Solar Association (BSW -Solar) in Berlin.

That means that solar energy in net electricity generation in Germany is likely to reach a record level of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year — almost 10 times the amount of electricity used by a major city like Hamburg in a year.

It is also almost 50 times as much as the 2.2 terawatt-hours generated byx solar power 20 years ago.

Carsten Körnig, the managing director of BSW-Solar, said the likely record was an important milestone as the world seeks to move away from climate-changing fossil fuels.

"Photovoltaics has developed from a niche technology into a cornerstone of our electricity supply," Körnig said.

"Society as a whole benefits from this: through cheaper electricity, fewer energy import and significantly lower climate-related damages," he said.

At 17.8% of total power generation, photovoltaics was the third most important energy source of domestically produced electricity behind wind power — the top energy source — followed by coal.

entries.title: Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
entries.summary: China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on the global stage.
entries.content:
China

Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit

November 15, 2026

China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on the global stage.

An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen this week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'?

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.

End of campaign to isolate Putin?

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.

"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.

She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.

"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.

Beijing and Moscow stick to 'no limits' partnership

Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.

At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.

China helping Russia from the sidelines

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.

While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.

Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.

What are the actual limits of China-Russia axis?

In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.

Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is  concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.

China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.

China getting a 'privileged vantage point' on Ukraine war

But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.

Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.

"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

entries.title: Could universal basic income be part of the solution in an AI economy?
entries.summary: The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists are not convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: How AI is likely to change the job market

November 15, 2026

The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists are not convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 "Digital Summit" in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July this year, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring last year, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

The impending job rupture

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world. This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socio-economic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

Why tech bosses love UBI

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the non-profit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of UBI.

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income (UBI) is very old: The English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances that they said AI would bring. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable.

Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

But Herrmann says it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She is not convinced that organizations like hers and people like Elon Musk want the same thing. "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

AI and basic income

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at Oxford University and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he told DW by email. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history: Partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact: AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socio-economic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she puts it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argues, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work: "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," Herrmann said. "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

entries.title: Tens of thousands continue to protest across France
entries.summary: Some 106,000 people marched through French cities for a fifth consecutive weekend of protests, marking the lowest turnout in recent weeks.
entries.content:
France

Tens of thousands continue to protest across France

November 15, 2026

Some 106,000 people marched through French cities for a fifth consecutive weekend of protests, marking the lowest turnout in recent weeks.

Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday to demonstrate against the rising cost of living and strained public services, the Interior Ministry said.

Saturday's demonstrations drew their lowest turnout in recent weeks. Some 106,000 people marched through French cities, with 24,000 in Paris alone. The previous weekend, some 146,000 people had participated nationwide.

The number of arrests was also significantly lower. Police detained 219 people across the country, according to the Interior Ministry.

Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful, police fired tear gas in Paris, Bordeaux and the western city of Nantes, including after some protesters shot fireworks.

France's protests expose deeper anger

Mass protests have swept across the European Union's second-largest economy for more than a month.

What began in September as student protests against teacher shortages and poor facilities has since evolved into a broader movement fuelled by anger over the rising cost of living, strained public services and police brutality.

In mid-October, around 565,000 people took to the streets across France, as riots, looting and clashes disrupted demonstrations in several cities.

As France entered its fifth consecutive weekend of nationwide unrest, President Emmanuel Macron's approval ratings fell to the lowest level since he took office in 2017, according to recent polls.

The French government doesn't have much room to respond to the protesters' demands due to its high debt.

entries.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
entries.summary: Eleven countries took part in the competition in Bangkok. Teenage winner Carmelle Collado's winning dance song is a tribute to Filipino women.
entries.content:
November 14, 2026

Eleven countries took part in the competition in Bangkok. Teenage winner Carmelle Collado's winning dance song is a tribute to Filipino women.

The Phillippines on Saturday became the first winner of the Asian version of the Eurovision Song Contest. 

Who took part in the event and which songs were featured?

Eleven countries, including South Korea, Malaysia and Vietnam, took part in the song contest in the Thai capital, Bangkok. However, major nations in the region such as China, Japan and India were absent from the event. 

19-year-old Carmelle Collado's dance song "Sobra-Sobra" (Too Much) won the competition. The song, which features lyrics in both English and Tagalog, is an empowering tribute to Filipino women.

The Philippines received 211 points in the competition, with Thailand in second place with 170 points. Vietnam placed third with 164 points, while Malaysia landed in fourth place on 152 points.

National juries in the participating countries and the viewing audience awarded the points.

The competition featured motifs inspired by host city Bangkok, with the participants making their way to the stage on tuk-tuks and waving the flag of the countries they represent in a parade.

Will the Eurovision Song Contest Asia become a sensation?

The contest featured some references to the camp European competition. Bulgarian singer Dara performed "Bangaranga," the song which won the Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna in May. 

It's unclear whether Eurovision Song Contest Asia will be as popular as the original competition, which received 131 million viewers this year. Tickets for the Bangkok event were still available just hours before it kicked off.

In 2022, a US spinoff, the American Song Contest, featured acts from all 50 US states. The competition, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg and American Idol star Kelly Clarkson, only lasted for one season.

entries.title: SpaceX carries out first-ever spaceship capture
entries.summary: The successful recovery of SpaceX's Starship marks a breakthrough in founder Elon Musk’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket system.
entries.content:
November 14, 2026

The successful recovery of SpaceX's Starship marks a breakthrough in founder Elon Musk’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket system.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from its longest-yet flight in orbit on Saturday to the tower it was launched from on Friday.

The spaceship descended and smoothly slipped between the mechanical "chopstick arms" above Launch Pad 2 in the US state of Texas. It was the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decadelong effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.

"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted. "Look at her! Baby, she’s back!"

SpaceX's Starship hit key milestone

It was the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system. The Starship spacecraft orbited Earth 14 times for over 22 hours, during which it deployed 26 Starlink satellites.

The successful return marked a ​key milestone in the multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees ​as crucial to SpaceX's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the Moon and eventually Mars.

NASA welcomed the news. The US space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. 

"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote on X.

SpaceX still investigating booster malfunction

SpaceX also intended to capture the bottom part of the rocket, known as the Super Heavy booster, but the lower stage recovery was aborted, and it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico shortly after launch on Friday.

SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon. The booster's guidance system sensed it was not in the correct position and initiated the self-destruction protocol. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX caught the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.

entries.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
entries.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

November 14, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.
